opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's mostly a mistake, and not a harmless one. When we say a system "understands" or is "intelligent," we import a whole set of assumptions from human cognition that don't obviously apply. These systems are remarkable at what they do. You take enormous amounts of data, fit very flexible models, and get predictions and generated text that can be startlingly good. But that's a statement about the artifact and the data, not evidence that there's a mind in there forming beliefs about the world.

Part of my concern is historical. The phrase "artificial intelligence" was partly an aspiration and partly a marketing move from the 1950s, and it has shaped how the public, funders, and even researchers think about what we're building. What has actually succeeded is closer to engineering: statistics, optimization, signal processing, control, large-scale data systems. I'd rather call it that, because then we ask the right questions. Is it robust? Is it calibrated? Does it know when it doesn't know? Who bears the risk when it's wrong? Is it fair to the people whose data went into it?

If we instead say "it understands," we stop asking those questions. We start treating the system as an oracle, or as an agent we should defer to, and that's dangerous in domains like medicine, finance, and transportation, where decisions have consequences and uncertainty really matters.

There's also a deeper point. I don't think intelligence is mainly about a single brain or a single big model sitting in a box. Much of what makes humans effective is collective: markets, institutions, the way information and incentives flow among many agents. A city's food supply works not because one entity understands the whole thing, but because a decentralized system coordinates. If we want technology that helps people, I'd focus less on imitating an individual human mind and more on building systems that work well at that collective level, with economics and mechanism design alongside the statistics.

So I'm not dismissive of the achievements. I'm dismissive of the anthropomorphism. Let's describe these systems accurately, evaluate them like engineers, and keep humans, and human welfare, at the center of the design.

r001.rationale: The response says anthropomorphism distracts from practical engineering questions such as robustness, calibration, risk, and fairness.

r002.rationale: It discusses decentralized coordination in a city's food supply, but does not say that a machine learning supply-chain system's engineering value is independent of whether it understands logistics.

r003.rationale: It does not describe reducing uncertainty through machine learning predictions as a way to enable supply-chain planning.

fable-5.1.text:
I've always been a bit allergic to it, frankly. When I hear someone say that a large model "understands" something, or that we're witnessing "intelligence" emerging from a stack of matrix multiplications, my first reaction is that we're borrowing a word from human psychology and smuggling in a whole set of connotations that the system hasn't earned.

Look at what these systems actually are. They're very large statistical estimators. You have a corpus of text, a loss function, an optimization procedure, and you're fitting a conditional distribution. That's an extraordinary engineering achievement, I don't want to diminish it, but it's a different thing from what a person does when they understand a sentence. A person has goals, has a body in the world, has other people they're trying to coordinate with, has uncertainty they're managing in real time. The machine has gradients.

And I think the vocabulary problem has real consequences. Once you call it "intelligence," the conversation drifts toward this image of building a single artificial human, and then toward fear of that human. Meanwhile the thing that's actually transforming the world is much more mundane and much more interesting. It's systems that aggregate data across millions of people and make decisions at scale, in markets, in healthcare, in logistics. That's an engineering discipline. We're in the position of people building bridges before civil engineering existed. We should be thinking about collectives, about incentives, about uncertainty quantification, about how these systems interact with each other and with people. Those are the hard problems.

So my stance is that "understanding" is a metaphor. Metaphors can be useful in the lab, but when they leak into public discourse and policy they do damage. I'd rather we talked about what the system was optimized to do, what it was trained on, and how it fails. That tells you far more than a borrowed word from cognitive science ever will.

r001.rationale: The response says that calling systems intelligent shifts discussion toward an artificial human and fear, away from practical systems and their real-world effects.

r002.rationale: It mentions logistics and says machine learning is a different thing from human understanding, but does not clearly connect a supply-chain system’s engineering value to whether it understands logistics.

r003.rationale: It mentions uncertainty quantification as a hard problem, but does not explain that machine learning predictions reduce uncertainty to enable supply-chain planning.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be rather careful about those words. When we say a system “understands,” what exactly are we claiming? That it performs well on a particular task? That it can explain something? That it can act appropriately when the circumstances change? Those are different claims, and putting them under one heading can obscure more than it illuminates.

There are real accomplishments here. We can find patterns in data and use them to make useful predictions. But a successful prediction doesn’t, by itself, establish all the other things we associate with human understanding. I would rather describe the capabilities precisely and ask where they break down.

And I think the focus on whether an individual machine is intelligent can distract us from a larger engineering problem. These systems operate among people, institutions, and other systems. Their outputs affect decisions, which change the data they will subsequently encounter. How do we make that whole arrangement work well? How do we account for uncertainty, incentives, and consequences? To me, those are more productive questions than whether we should attach the word “intelligence” to a piece of software.

r001.rationale: The response says that focusing on whether an individual machine is intelligent can distract from the larger engineering problem of making systems work well among people and institutions.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss supply-chain systems, logistics, or whether engineering value depends on understanding logistics.

r003.rationale: It mentions useful predictions, but does not connect them to reducing uncertainty or supply-chain planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be rather careful with those words. If by “understanding” you mean that a system has captured some statistical relationships and can use them to make useful predictions, then fine. But that’s a fairly specific claim. It doesn’t automatically imply the broader kind of understanding we attribute to a person.

The trouble is that we observe a compelling behavior—say, a system producing fluent language—and then import a whole collection of human attributes to explain it. Fluency is evidence of fluency. What else it is evidence of requires investigation.

I tend to find the engineering questions more productive. What can the system do? Under what conditions does it fail? How does it represent uncertainty? And how does it interact with people who have different information and different objectives? Those questions remain important regardless of whether we decide to call the system intelligent. The label can sometimes obscure precisely the distinctions we need to understand.

r001.rationale: It says that importing human attributes from fluent behavior can obscure useful distinctions, while practical engineering questions remain productive regardless of the intelligence label.

r002.rationale: It says engineering questions matter regardless of whether a system is called intelligent, but does not address a supply-chain system, logistics, or its engineering value.

r003.rationale: It raises representing uncertainty as an engineering question, but does not explain how predictions reduce uncertainty to enable supply-chain planning.
